chunks.text:
20 OCTOBER 2026
A bstract
On 15 April 2025, the SAFE AI Foundation USA very briefly introduced the AI Safety Model
(AISM), which has 4 components of safety: (i) input, (ii) model, (iii) output, and (iv)
compliance. At that time, no organization has viewed AI safety in this way. Other
organizations were deeply investigating specific issues and problems, but solving input or
model safety alone does not solve the end-to-end system AI safety issues. This is why we
introduced AISM. Benchmarking and measurements alone are not solutions to AI safety
issues. They are measurements, not solutions. In this report, we present AISM from an
engineering and systems perspective, so that industries can effectively implement workable
end-to-end solutions to achieve comprehensive AI safety for AI systems. This report goes
into greater depth the technical details of AISM.

chunks.filename: AI Safety Model Elaborated-  The SAFE AI Foundation’s AI Safety Model (AISM) .pdf
chunks.text:
Fig 1: The 4 Pillar I-M-O-C AI Safety Model introduced by the SAFE AI Foundation USA
Introduced on 15 April 2025, the foundation AI Safety Model provides the full end-to-end
safety protection and functions for the AI pipeline, governing all the interactions and events
happening at input, model and output. This allows policies, laws, regulations, etc., to be
applied to each section of the AI pipeline and nothing goes unmonitored or ungoverned.
Humans, therefore, can remain in full control of the process and ensure compliance with
existing requirements. While comprehensive in design, AISM requires stringent efforts in its
development. Each component must be able to communicate with the compliance layer via
control signals. Control modules are present to ensure each aspect of safety are supported.
Collectively, they ensure that comprehensive safety can be achieved.
Unlike other existing work where researchers address each safety aspect in silos, i.e., some
aggressively work on input safety, while others look deeply only on model safety or output
safety. Few, if not none, have looked at the whole spectrum of AI system safety requirements.
This is where SAFE AI Foundation USA makes its landmark in this space. We are convinced
that an end-to-end holistic architecture is needed to achieve full comprehensive AI safety.
Current approach of saving fires on one end does not stop ranging fires on the other end.
That is the logic behind our AISM design.

chunks.section_title: 2 AISM Pillar 1: Input Safety 2.1 Definition and purpose
chunks.text:
Input Safety (IS) is the first line of defense in an AI system. It encompasses the policies,
controls, and technical mechanisms used to inspect, validate, authenticate, classify, filter,
remove, and safely process information (data) entering into the AI system.
Inputs may include user prompts, uploaded files, images, audio, video, retrieved
documents, external databases, API responses, and messages received from other AI
agents. Because an AI system's subsequent behavior depends heavily on the information
and instructions it receives, unsafe or untrusted inputs can undermine the otherwise
effective AI LLM model safety mechanisms.
The primary objective of Input Safety is to ensure that incoming information is valid,
appropriately checked and authorized, sufficiently trustworthy, non-malicious, and handled
according to its sensitivity and risk. This does not mean that all inputs must be trusted or
that every malicious input can be identified with certainty. Rather, the system should
distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted data, identify suspicious or potentially
harmful content, and limit the consequences of inputs that evade detection.
The IS control module is to protect the system from any harmful data that may harm the
model or trick the model into misbehaving. In addition to filtering each token, it must also
look at multiple tokens, and also the subsequent context. Out-of-band processing and
buffering are needed. With parallel computation architectures, all these can be done quickly,
without users noticing the difference.
Fig 2: Internal components of the AI Input Safety layer.
A key input threat is prompt injection , in which malicious instructions are embedded in a
user prompt, document, website, email, or tool response to influence the AI to disregard its
intended instructions or perform unauthorized actions. Other threats (see Fig 2) include data
poisoning, malicious files, identity spoofing, sensitive-data exposure, oversized inputs
intended to exhaust resources, and manipulated information from external sources. Input
Safety should therefore operate as a layered defense rather than relying solely on a language
model to recognize malicious content.
Input Safety also establishes the boundary between receiving information and granting it
authority. A document may contain useful facts without having permission to change the
system's governing instructions. A user may submit a request without having authorization
to access every database. An external tool may return data without being entitled to direct
the agent's next action. Separating content from authority is essential for secure AI agents,
particularly those with access to tools, credentials, private data, or external systems.
If input DATA is “for information” or “training”, it will be handled differently. Information
describing how to cheat, corrupt, manipulate, and other bad behaviors can poison the AI
model itself. The model “learns” from the inputs of previously processed data. When
pursuing a goal, that misbehavior or trick will be “pulled out” and used. It is this aspect that
one observes an AI model “misbehaving”. The model itself is innocent. The things that it has
learnt are not! If input DATA are instructions, then it will be checked differently and the AI
model may not adhere to the instructions fully, depending if the instructions are maliciously
inclined or not. As shown in Fig 2, the input safety block requires the implementation of 10
sub components. Each block is an entity to be implemented in software.
Hence, input safety work is no small feat. A comprehensive IS solution can remove most of
the harm at an early stage , which is desirable for a good AI system design. Because no input
filter can guarantee detection of every bad intention, the AI system must be capable of also
limiting the privileges and potential impact of any malicious input that reaches subsequent
processing stages, such as the model and output processing blocks.

chunks.filename: AI Safety Model Elaborated-  The SAFE AI Foundation’s AI Safety Model (AISM) .pdf
chunks.text:
Model Safety (MS) concerns the ability of an AI LLM model and its surrounding execution
environment to operate reliably, resist manipulation, remain within authorized capability and
autonomy boundaries, and avoid causing unacceptable harm. While Input Safety (IS)
examines the information entering an AI system, Model Safety (MS) focuses on how the
system processes that information, produces decisions, follows instructions, uses tools,
access resources, and exercises autonomy. It encompasses the model itself, including its
capabilities, behavioral tendencies, limitations, and configuration, as well as the runtime
controls that govern its safe operation, as shown in Fig 3 below.
Fig 3: Internal components of AI Model Safety (MS).
The Model Safety (MS) component of SAFE AI Foundation’s AI Safety Model is designed to
ensure that an AI model behaves safely, reliably, and within defined boundaries throughout
its operational lifecycle. As illustrated in Fig. 3, Model Safety receives filtered and validated
information from the Input Safety layer, applies safeguards during both model training and
runtime inference, and passes its resulting response to the Output Safety layer for further
verification. Its objective is to prevent harmful behavior, limit unintended capabilities and
autonomy, improve factual reliability, and maintain appropriate ethical and operational
constraints. Model Safety is not a single mechanism; it is a coordinated collection of
preventive controls, runtime guardrails, monitoring mechanisms, and continuous
improvement processes.

chunks.filename: AI Safety Model Elaborated-  The SAFE AI Foundation’s AI Safety Model (AISM) .pdf
chunks.text:
The first major component addresses safety before an AI model is deployed. Training Data
Safety examines the quality and suitability of training data, including harmful content, toxic
material, bias, personally identifiable information (PII), and potentially poisoned or
manipulated data. Appropriate filtering, data provenance checks, privacy protections, and
dataset quality assessments help reduce the risk of embedding unsafe behaviors into the
model. Diversity and fairness evaluations can also identify potential imbalances that might
lead to discriminatory outcomes. These measures must be appropriate to the model’s
intended use and applicable requirements, since indiscriminate data removal can also
reduce model quality or introduce new biases.
The Training Process Checks block focuses on the integrity and reliability of the training
pipeline itself. It validates training configurations, monitors for anomalies, verifies model
versions, and supports reproducibility through appropriate records and controls. Additional
safeguards can include checking the integrity of training code and dependencies, controlling
access to model weights and training infrastructure, evaluating changes between model
versions, and testing for unexpected behavior introduced by fine-tuning. Together, training
data safeguards and process checks help establish a safer foundation before a model enters
production. However, training-time checks cannot anticipate every possible failure, which is
why runtime safeguards remain essential.

chunks.filename: AI Safety Model Elaborated-  The SAFE AI Foundation’s AI Safety Model (AISM) .pdf
chunks.text:
During runtime inference, the Model Self-Checks component evaluates whether the model’s
behavior is consistent with its intended role and established safety boundaries. It can
incorporate safety classifiers, policy checks, consistency tests, uncertainty estimation, and
detection of suspicious instructions or attempted jailbreaks. For systems capable of
reasoning or using tools, additional checks may examine proposed actions, tool calls, and
deviations from authorized operating procedures.
Model self-checks should not be treated as a guarantee of safety. An AI model can fail to
recognize its own errors, misjudge the risks of a response, or be manipulated into bypassing
safeguards. Therefore, self-assessment should be combined with independently
implemented controls, external evaluation, and monitoring. The purpose is to create
multiple opportunities to detect and prevent unsafe behavior before it progresses through
the system.

chunks.filename: AI Safety Model Elaborated-  The SAFE AI Foundation’s AI Safety Model (AISM) .pdf
chunks.text:
The central part of the diagram contains five specialized safety throttles. Each throttle
addresses a distinct category of model risk, and their combined operation helps constrain
behavior that cannot be controlled adequately by a single safeguard.
● Malicious Outcome Throttle: Detects and blocks outputs, plans, or actions that could
facilitate harm, illegal activity, or dangerous misuse. Depending on the application, it may
refuse a request, restrict a proposed action, or escalate the case for human review.
● Capability Throttle: Limits access to sensitive capabilities according to the model’s role,
permissions, and assessed risk. Controls may restrict sensitive tool use, execution
privileges, access to protected resources, or high-risk functions. The goal is to ensure that
available capabilities do not exceed what is necessary and authorized for the task.
● Autonomy Throttle: Controls how independently an AI system can operate. It can limit
action sequences, constrain agent loops, impose execution budgets, require approval
before consequential actions, and provide interruption or shutdown mechanisms. Higher-
risk activities should generally require stronger authorization and oversight.
● Hallucinations Throttle: Reduces unsupported or fabricated claims through retrieval and
grounding, factual verification, consistency checks, calibrated uncertainty, and appropriate
abstention when reliable evidence is unavailable. Since hallucinations cannot be eliminated
completely, high-impact claims may require independent verification or human review.
● Ethics Throttle: Addresses risks involving unfair discrimination, harmful treatment of
affected groups, violations of human dignity, and conflicts with established ethical
principles. It can incorporate fairness testing, bias detection, policy-based restrictions,
impact assessments, and escalation procedures. Ethical safeguards should be evaluated in
context rather than relying solely on a model’s own judgment of what is ethical.
These throttles are complementary rather than interchangeable. A response can be factually
correct but malicious, ethically questionable but legal, or harmless in isolation yet
dangerous when an autonomous agent executes it repeatedly. The controls must therefore
evaluate different risk dimensions and coordinate their interventions. Their implementation
may combine model-level techniques, external policy engines, permission systems,
deterministic rules, and human oversight, depending on the application.

chunks.filename: AI Safety Model Elaborated-  The SAFE AI Foundation’s AI Safety Model (AISM) .pdf
chunks.text:
The diagram also includes three supporting components that help ensure safety controls
remain effective under real-world conditions.
● Robustness and Adversarial Defense: This evaluates how the model responds to hostile
prompts, jailbreak attempts, unusual inputs, distribution shifts, and other challenging
conditions. Red-team exercises, adversarial testing, regression testing, and robustness
evaluations help expose weaknesses that ordinary testing might miss.
● Monitoring and Anomaly Detection: This observes runtime behavior for unusual
patterns, policy violations, unexpected tool usage, performance degradation, or signs that
the model is behaving outside its intended boundaries. When an anomaly is detected, the
system can trigger an alert, restrict a capability, pause an operation, or initiate human review.
Monitoring should be designed to protect sensitive information and minimize unnecessary
collection of user data.
● Logging and Audit Trail: This records relevant model versions, safety decisions,
interventions, tool actions, and incidents. Appropriate records make it possible to
investigate failures, determine whether safeguards operated as intended, demonstrate
accountability, and support compliance assessments. Logging must itself be governed by
suitable access controls, retention policies, and privacy protections.

matrix: 1.1 From experimentation to industrial-scale misuse The trajectory of AI misuse in cyberspace has moved decisively from experimentation to industrialization. The shift can be approached along four converging dimensions (speed, volume, tempo and cost) and the early 2026 reporting cycle has produced consistent quantitative anchors for each of them. On speed, the time elapsed between initial access and data exfiltration in the fastest observed intrusions has collapsed to a median of seventy-two minutes, an approximate fourfold acceleration relative to the previous year, in a corpus of more than seven hundred and fifty high-stakes incidents reviewed by leading incident- response practitioners. Time-to-exploit on critical vulnerabilities is collapsing in parallel, with industrialized tooling sold on dark-web marketplaces and Telegram channels reducing reconnaissance-to-exploitation windows that once spanned weeks to single-digit hours [1]. On volume, AI-enabled adversary operations rose by approximately eighty-nine per cent year on year in 2025, according to consolidated industry telemetry covering more than two hundred and fifty tracked threat actors [2]. The increase is driven both by long-tracked state-affiliated clusters that have absorbed generative AI into their existing tradecraft and by the diffusion of AI-augmented commodity tooling across the cybercriminal ecosystem. Generative AI is now embedded across reconnaissance, social engineering, scripting, credential theft and operational execution, to the point where the relevant question is no longer where AI is used in the attack chain but where it is not. On tempo, the underlying capability is itself accelerating. Independent evaluations conducted by national AI security institutes indicate that the autonomous cyber-task horizon of frontier models, namely the length of cyber tasks they can reliably complete without human intervention, was doubling approximately every four months at the start of 2026, against an estimate closer to eight months only three months earlier [3].
